# Use as a submodule

The repository is written so that it works two ways: on its own, driven by
`analyses.yml`, and as a component of a larger GWF project that adds this repository
as a Git submodule and grafts the iTRAILS targets onto its own workflow. The second
is the reason the pipeline is factored the way it is.

Submodules are useful when an analysis component is shared across projects, or when
several pipelines need to be combined into one dependency graph. Each component keeps
its own repository, environment and workflow, and the parent decides how they connect;
the GWF documentation describes the underlying patterns for
[dynamically generated workflows](https://gwf.app/guide/patterns/#dynamically-generating-a-workflow)
and [large workflows](https://gwf.app/guide/patterns/#large-workflows).

## Add the component

From the root of the parent project:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
git submodule add git@github.com:munch-group/itrails.git itrails
git submodule init itrails
git submodule update itrails
git add .gitmodules itrails
git commit -m 'Added itrails as submodule'
```

Then check out a branch inside the submodule. A fresh submodule is in detached HEAD
state, and work committed there is easy to lose:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
cd itrails
git checkout main
```

::: { .callout-important }

Install a current Git in your environment — the one on the cluster is ancient — and
set these once, since the commands below assume them:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
git config --global diff.submodule log
git config status.submodulesummary 1
git config push.recurseSubmodules check
```

:::

## Call the factory

The parent imports `itrails_workflow` and hands it its own `Workflow` object:

```python
import os, sys
from gwf import Workflow

gwf = Workflow(defaults={'account': 'my-project'})

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), 'itrails'))
from itrails_workflow import itrails_workflow

gwf, itrails_targets = itrails_workflow(
    gwf=gwf,
    analyses=[
        dict(name='primates',
             maf='data/alignment.maf',
             config='config/itrails_config.yaml',
             window_size=2_000_000),
    ],
    output_dir='steps/itrails',
)
```

::: { .callout-note }

## Why the odd import

The factory lives in `itrails_workflow.py` rather than `workflow.py`, and is imported
by inserting the submodule directory on `sys.path`. Both choices avoid name
collisions: the parent has its own `workflow.py`, and the *installed Python package*
is also called `itrails`, so importing this repository as a package would shadow the
tool it wraps.

:::

Paths in the analysis dictionaries are resolved relative to where `gwf run` is
invoked — the parent project root — not relative to the submodule.

## Arguments

| Argument | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| `gwf` | the parent's `Workflow`; a new one is created if omitted |
| `analyses` | list of analysis dictionaries, the same keys as in `analyses.yml` |
| `output_dir` | root for all output, default `steps/itrails` |
| `account` | Slurm account added to every target |
| `window_size`, `fit` | defaults for all analyses, overridable per analysis |
| `run_prefix` | command prefix that puts the iTRAILS executables on `PATH` |
| `*_options` | per-step resource dictionaries applied to every analysis |

`run_prefix` defaults to running each command inside the submodule's own pixi
environment, resolved from the module's own location so that it works no matter which
directory the parent is run from. A parent that already provides iTRAILS can pass its
own activation prefix, or `run_prefix=''` to use whatever is on `PATH`.

## Wiring up downstream targets

The factory returns `(gwf, targets)`, where `targets` maps step names to the created
targets, so the parent can depend on iTRAILS output by name instead of by hard-coded
path:

```python
viterbi_csv = itrails_targets['concat_viterbi'][0].outputs['csv']
best_model = itrails_targets['optimize'][0].outputs['best_model']

gwf.target('summarize',
           inputs=[viterbi_csv],
           outputs=['steps/summary/ils_fractions.tsv']) << f"""
python scripts/summarize_ils.py {viterbi_csv} steps/summary/ils_fractions.tsv
"""
```

The keys are `optimize`, `viterbi` and `posterior`; `vcf2maf` when the analysis
starts from VCFs; and `split`, `concat_viterbi` and `concat_posterior` for windowed
analyses. Each target's `outputs` dictionary is documented in
[Output files](outputs.qmd) — `best_model`, `viterbi`, `posterior`, `hidden_states`,
`maf`, `windows`, `manifest`, `blocks` and `csv`.

Feeding a parent-generated alignment *into* the component works the same way, with
one caveat: a windowed analysis reading a `maf` needs that file to exist when the
workflow is defined, so run the target that produces it first. VCF analyses have no
such constraint — see [Windowed analyses](windowing.qmd).

## Several components in one workflow

Components combine by passing the same `gwf` object to each factory, which is how
this repository is meant to sit alongside sibling components such as `rfmix`:

```python
import os, sys
from gwf import Workflow

def target_output_files(targets, key):
    return [out for target in targets[key] for out in target.outputs]

gwf = Workflow(defaults={'account': 'my-project'})

for component in ['itrails', 'rfmix']:
    sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), component))

from itrails_workflow import itrails_workflow
from workflow import rfmix_workflow

gwf, itrails_targets = itrails_workflow(gwf=gwf, analyses=[...],
                                        output_dir='steps/itrails')
gwf, rfmix_targets = rfmix_workflow(gwf, analyzes=[...],
                                    output_dir='steps/rfmix')
```

Since every target ends up in one graph, GWF works out the dependencies across
components from the files they declare, and `gwf status` shows the whole pipeline.

## Keeping the submodule current

Pulling in the parent updates the *recorded state* of the submodule but does not
update the submodule contents; that is a separate step:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
git pull                                  # parent, including the recorded commit
git submodule update --remote --merge     # fetch and merge submodule changes
```

`--checkout` (the default) puts the submodule on a detached HEAD at the recorded
commit, `--merge` merges into the current branch, and `--rebase` rebases onto it.
Changes made inside the submodule are published from within it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
cd itrails
git add -u && git commit -m 'Adjusted resources'
git push
```

Then commit the new submodule state in the parent, which is what records the version
of the component the project used.
